items: Nutrition failure: weight falls first; endocrine disease: height slows with preserved/increased weight
★ Falling **2 major percentile channels**, well child → **diet diary, calorie counts** before labs
Correct prematurity through about 2 years; track infant head circumference

rows.label: Use when
items: Developmental surveillance every visit; standardized general screens at 9, 18, and 30 months
★ **Regression/missed milestones → early intervention**; language delay → **audiometry** before speech testing
BMI-for-age from 2 years; weight-for-length younger; consider parental heights and pubertal timing

rows.label: Compare
items: Tantrums, picky eating, bedtime separation distress → reassure, routines, calm limits; no sedatives
Head banging at sleep onset or frustration, normal development → self-soothing; assess injuries
Preschool restlessness, good function → no stimulants; overwhelmed parent → **parenting classes**

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **One percentile cannot diagnose disease**; stable tracking + normal exam → reassure
Persistent skill loss needs evaluation; never wait for school failure
Short parents, normal bone age → familial; average parents, delayed puberty → **constitutional delay**

rows.label: Adolescence
items: ★ Moodiness, privacy, family detachment, rule-questioning, late bedtimes, good function → reassure, educate parents
Parental-pressure conflict, occasional experimentation, no impairment → not ODD, substance use disorder
Weight worry, stable percentile, normal BMI, regular menses → normal; not eating disorder

table.title: Normal by age
rows: Holds head up; not yet reaching
Sits unsupported; bangs blocks, self-feeds finger foods
Walks; scribbles; non-walker at 14 months normal
Balances on one foot; copies circle
Same-sex parent preference; involve other parent otherwise

child-growth-and-development.evidence: Checked screening ages 2026-10-30: [AAP surveillance/screening](https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/); growth facts established pediatric teaching.

childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.name: Childhood and adolescent immunizations
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.scope: Routine pediatric vaccine schedule, adolescent immunizations (meningococcal conjugate, HPV, Tdap), catch-up vaccination guidelines
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.core: Vaccinate before exposure; use age, prior doses, minimum intervals, and immune status to choose the next dose.

rows.label: Who
items: All children; AAP 2026 schedule retains broad routine childhood protection

rows.label: Schedule
items: ★ 11–12 years: **Tdap, MenACWY**; MenACWY booster at 16 years
AAP HPV: start 9–12 years; <15 years → two doses, 6–12 months apart
HPV initiation ≥15 years or immunocompromised → three doses at 0, 1–2, 6 months

rows.label: Special groups
items: ★ Catch-up: **never restart**; respect minimum ages and intervals
Asplenia/complement defects: extra meningococcal/pneumococcal doses; annual influenza from 6 months
HBsAg-positive mother: HepB vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth

rows.label: Choice
items: MenB: shared decision, usually 16–23 years; high-risk patients need earlier protection

rows.label: Contraindications
items: ★ Live vaccines: pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency; **conjugates (Hib) still indicated**; prior anaphylaxis: no repeat
Rotavirus: SCID, prior intussusception; first dose ≤14 weeks 6 days; finish by 8 months

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **AAP/classic boards: multidose HPV**; federal 2026 policy: one dose
Preterm → **chronological age, full dose**; mild illness, antibiotics, breastfeeding → vaccinate
Separate injectable live vaccines ≥4 weeks unless simultaneous; IVIG can delay MMR/varicella

table.title: Routine AAP childhood schedule
rows: First vaccination <9 years: two ≥4 weeks apart

colorectal-carcinoma.name: Colorectal carcinoma
colorectal-carcinoma.scope: Colon adenocarcinoma, rectal cancer, staging, surgical resection (hemicolectomy), liver metastases, chemotherapy
colorectal-carcinoma.core: Occult blood loss, altered bowel habits, or obstruction warrants colon evaluation; cancer stage determines local and systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, adenomas, Lynch/FAP, longstanding colitis, family history; smoking, obesity, processed meat

rows.label: Clues
items: Right-sided lesions → iron-deficiency anemia, fatigue, occult bleeding
Left-sided lesions → constipation, narrowed stools, obstruction; rectal lesions → tenesmus/hematochezia
Weight loss, palpable mass; hepatomegaly or elevated ALP suggests hepatic spread
Bladder invasion → colovesical fistula: fecaluria, mixed fecal flora in urine

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Adenoma–carcinoma sequence involves APC, KRAS, p53; mismatch-repair failure drives microsatellite instability
Portal drainage favors liver metastases; distal rectal tumors may spread directly to lungs

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Colonoscopy with biopsy**; evaluate entire colon for synchronous tumors
★ Confirmed cancer → **CT chest/abdomen/pelvis**, baseline CEA, tumor mismatch-repair/MSI testing
Rectal cancer → pelvic MRI for local staging; CEA cannot diagnose or screen
Obstruction/perforation → urgent contrast CT and surgical assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable colon cancer → **segmental colectomy with lymphadenectomy**; selected liver metastases → resection
Stage III → adjuvant FOLFOX/CAPOX; selected high-risk stage II → individualized chemotherapy
Locally advanced rectal cancer → neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy/chemoradiation, then total mesorectal excision
Unresectable metastases, nonobstructing primary → **chemotherapy**, no primary resection; MSI-high → checkpoint inhibitor
Perforation or unstable obstruction → urgent operation; selected stable obstruction → stent or diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Bleeding, perforation, malignant obstruction; venous thrombosis; oxaliplatin neuropathy
Postoperative anastomotic leak; pelvic treatment → urinary/sexual dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Average-risk screening **45–75 years**; earlier colonoscopy for strong family history/hereditary syndromes
Postresection colonoscopy, CEA and stage-based CT surveillance; remove premalignant polyps

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hemorrhoids: outlet bleeding without explanatory anemia; do not dismiss alarm features
IBD: chronic inflammatory diarrhea; diverticulitis: acute focal pain and fever

colorectal-carcinoma.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF colorectal screening](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/colorectal-cancer-screening); treatment: established oncology teaching.

table.title: TNM essentials
rows: Extension through muscle; no regional nodal spread

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

congenital-infections.name: Congenital infections
congenital-infections.scope: Cytomegalovirus (sensorineural hearing loss, periventricular calcifications), Toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis), Parvovirus B19 (hydrops), Rubella, Varicella, Zika, screening and diagnosis
congenital-infections.core: Congenital infection causes growth restriction, hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, thrombocytopenia, or hydrops; organ-specific patterns identify the pathogen.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CMV: toddler saliva/urine; toxoplasma: undercooked meat, cat feces; B19: child with slapped-cheek rash
Absent rubella/varicella immunity; mosquito exposure or sexual transmission in Zika-risk areas

rows.label: Clues
items: Petechiae/blueberry-muffin lesions, abnormal fetal ultrasound; many infected newborns initially appear well
★ B19 hydrops: cardiomegaly, ascites, edema without red-cell alloantibodies
Maternal rash: B19 → slapped cheek, then reticular limb rash; rubella → descending rash, postauricular nodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transplacental infection disrupts organogenesis; later exposure may cause inflammation or marrow suppression
Toxoplasma transmission increases with gestational age; earlier infection causes more severe injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Maternal exposure → pathogen-specific **IgG/IgM**, paired titers or avidity; isolated IgM needs confirmation
★ CMV newborn diagnosis: saliva PCR then confirm urine PCR **within 21 days**
Suspected fetal infection → targeted ultrasound, pathogen-specific amniotic-fluid PCR; B19 → serial MCA Doppler
Prenatal rubella IgG routinely; no universal US maternal CMV, toxoplasma, or B19 screening

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic congenital CMV → **valganciclovir**, monitor CBC and liver tests
Congenital toxoplasmosis → pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin; maternal regimen depends on fetal infection
B19 severe fetal anemia → intrauterine transfusion; rubella/Zika structural injury → supportive care
Maternal varicella exposure without immunity → varicella-zoster immune globulin; maternal pneumonia → IV acyclovir
Maternal varicella onset 5 days before to 2 days after delivery → **newborn VZIG**

rows.label: Complications
items: Stillbirth, neurodevelopmental disability; delayed/progressive hearing loss requires longitudinal audiology

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Rubella/varicella vaccination before pregnancy or postpartum; **live vaccines contraindicated during pregnancy**
Handwashing after diapers; cook meat, avoid litter handling; mosquito precautions and Zika exposure counseling
Term newborn of varicella-immune mother: transplacental IgG protects → no prophylaxis after exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aneuploidy: abnormal genetic testing rather than pathogen testing
Rh disease: positive maternal antibody screen with fetal anemia

table.title: Discriminating congenital patterns
rows: Periventricular calcifications, microcephaly, sensorineural hearing loss, chorioretinitis
Severe microcephaly, subcortical calcifications, ocular abnormalities

congenital-infections.evidence: CMV testing checked 2026-10-30: [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/cytomegalovirus/hcp/clinical-overview/index.html); remaining pathogen patterns established teaching.

conjunctivitis.name: Conjunctivitis
conjunctivitis.scope: Viral conjunctivitis, bacterial conjunctivitis, allergic conjunctivitis, contact lens-associated keratitis, hygiene and transmission precautions
conjunctivitis.core: A red eye with discharge and preserved vision usually reflects conjunctivitis; significant pain, photophobia, or visual loss requires corneal/ocular evaluation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent respiratory infection, sick contacts, daycare; seasonal allergens and atopy
Contact lenses, poor lens hygiene; sexual exposure with hyperpurulent or persistent disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Gritty sensation, diffuse conjunctival injection; pupils and visual acuity generally normal
★ **Severe pain, photophobia, corneal opacity, reduced vision** → urgent ophthalmology
Copious rapidly recurring pus → gonococcus; chronic follicular disease → chlamydia

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Conjunctival inflammation causes vascular dilation and exudate without primary intraocular inflammation
IgE-mediated mast-cell activation drives allergen-associated itching

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Visual acuity first**; inspect pupils, cornea, discharge, preauricular nodes
Fluorescein staining for pain, foreign-body sensation, or lens use; dendrites suggest HSV
Cultures/NAAT for hyperacute purulence, neonatal infection, recurrent or treatment-resistant presentations

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Contact lens use + painful red eye** → remove lenses, urgent keratitis evaluation
Suspected bacterial corneal infection → topical fluoroquinolone with Pseudomonas coverage under ophthalmology
Gonococcal disease → systemic ceftriaxone, irrigation, STI evaluation; topical drops alone insufficient
Chlamydial disease → systemic doxycycline, partner treatment; avoid empiric topical steroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Keratitis, corneal ulceration, scarring; gonococcus can rapidly perforate the cornea
Topical steroid misuse can worsen herpetic infection and raise intraocular pressure

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Handwashing, no shared towels/cosmetics**, avoid eye rubbing; viral disease highly contagious
Discard contaminated lenses/case; avoid swimming or sleeping in lenses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anterior uveitis: consensual photophobia, ciliary flush, cells/flare
Acute angle closure: high IOP, headache/nausea, fixed mid-dilated pupil
Subconjunctival hemorrhage: sharply demarcated blood, no discharge or discomfort; normal vision/exam → **reassurance only**

table.title: Common uncomplicated forms
rows: Watery; URI; preauricular nodes; morning crusting possible

conjunctivitis.evidence: Not checked online; established ophthalmology teaching.

costochondritis.name: Costochondritis
costochondritis.scope: Costosternal syndrome, Tietze syndrome, reproducible chest wall tenderness, differential diagnosis of chest pain, conservative management
costochondritis.core: Localized anterior chest discomfort reproducible over costochondral joints commonly reflects a benign inflammatory chest-wall syndrome after dangerous causes are excluded.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Repetitive upper-body activity, lifting, forceful coughing, recent respiratory infection; often no clear trigger
Tietze syndrome usually younger adults; infectious cartilage disease with injection drug use or thoracic procedures

rows.label: Clues
items: Sharp or aching parasternal pain, worsened by deep breathing, twisting or arm movement
★ Tender second–fifth costosternal junctions; **normal cardiopulmonary examination** in uncomplicated cases
Exertional pressure, syncope, hypoxemia, fever or hemodynamic instability → evaluate another cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Local mechanical strain and inflammation affect costochondral/costosternal structures; cartilage usually remains intact

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** after history, cardiopulmonary examination and risk assessment
Possible ACS → ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponins; tenderness alone cannot exclude infarction
Chest radiograph for pulmonary findings, trauma or suspected infection; no routine imaging for uncomplicated cases
Focal warmth, erythema, fever → CBC/inflammatory markers and evaluation for septic costochondritis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NSAIDs or topical diclofenac**, heat, temporary reduction of provoking activities
Acetaminophen when NSAIDs unsuitable; gradual return to activity, stretching/physical rehabilitation for persistence
Rare refractory focal symptoms → local glucocorticoid injection after excluding infection
Reassurance after evaluation; antibiotics reserved for proven/suspected bacterial infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Usually self-limited over weeks; recurrent discomfort or activity restriction
NSAIDs → GI bleeding, AKI; persistent/worsening pain warrants diagnostic reassessment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Ergonomic modification, graded exercise, cough control; avoid repeated strain during recovery

rows.label: Mimics
items: ACS: ischemic ECG/troponin changes or typical exertional pattern
PE: dyspnea, tachycardia, VTE risk; pericarditis: positional pain, diffuse ST elevation

costochondritis.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

table.title: Chest-wall patterns
rows: Visible swelling, often one upper junction

delirium.name: Delirium
delirium.scope: Diagnostic criteria, precipitating causes (infection, metabolic, drugs), workup, management and prevention
delirium.core: Acute fluctuating inattention with altered cognition or awareness indicates delirium and requires a search for physiologic triggers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, baseline dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, hospitalization or recent surgery
Infection (UTI, pneumonia, wound), hypoxia, metabolic derangement, dehydration, retention, constipation and uncontrolled pain
Anticholinergics (amitriptyline), meperidine, other opioids, steroids, sedatives; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal

rows.label: Clues
items: Disorganized thinking, sleep–wake reversal, hallucinations; hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed presentation
★ Hypoactive withdrawal/lethargy easily missed; **test attention**, not orientation alone
Digit span, months backward or inability to sustain conversation reveals attentional deficit
**Asterixis** → toxic-metabolic encephalopathy of any cause, not only hepatic failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Systemic stress and drug effects disrupt vulnerable brain networks and neurotransmitter balance
Multiple small precipitating factors can exceed low cognitive reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CAM**: acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Immediate glucose, oxygenation, vitals; focused neurologic examination, medication review and collateral baseline
CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function; ECG, chest imaging guided by findings; wound/sepsis signs → **blood cultures**
CT head for focal deficit, trauma or unexplained reduced consciousness; LP for suspected CNS infection
Fever, urinary symptoms or dementia → **urinalysis** for UTI before CT/LP; bacteriuria alone doesn't prove cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat precipitant**; reorient, restore hearing/glasses, hydrate, mobilize and normalize sleep
Calm environment and familiar support; remove unnecessary catheters and avoid physical restraints
★ Severe distress or danger despite de-escalation → short course **haloperidol**, check QT/EPS risk
Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia → avoid potent dopamine blockers; specialist-guided alternative
Benzodiazepines generally worsen delirium; reserve for withdrawal or selected seizures/catatonia

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, persistent cognitive impairment and increased mortality
Antipsychotics may prolong QT; sedation may conceal clinical deterioration

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Multicomponent prevention: orientation, daytime activity, sleep protection, hydration, pain control and drug review
Minimize nighttime interruptions and unnecessary sedatives; encourage family engagement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: chronic progression; attention relatively preserved early
Depression: sustained mood symptoms without fluctuating consciousness
Primary psychosis: usually preserved attention and alertness

depressive-disorders.name: Depressive disorders
depressive-disorders.scope: Major depressive disorder criteria, depression in older adults, bereavement vs MDD, pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, suicide risk
depressive-disorders.core: Persistent low mood or loss of pleasure with neurovegetative and cognitive symptoms, causing clinically significant distress or impaired function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior episodes, family history, chronic illness/pain, substance use, postpartum period, social isolation
Older adults: disability, bereavement, polypharmacy; somatic presentations

rows.label: Clues
items: SIGECAPS: sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor change, suicidality
Psychotic depression: delusions/hallucinations only during mood episodes, often guilt or nihilism
★ **Suicide risk**: prior attempt, intent, plan, means, agitation, psychosis, intoxication
Youth: **irritable mood** qualifies; academic decline, withdrawal, somatic complaints; not normal teenage behavior

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Multifactorial mood-circuit dysfunction involving monoamines, **HPA hyperactivity with raised cortisol**, and neuroplasticity

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ MDD: **≥5 symptoms for ≥2 weeks**, including depressed mood or anhedonia; exclude mania/hypomania
Screen all adults, even asymptomatic: PHQ-2, PHQ-9 for severity; older adults: **Geriatric Depression Scale**
Interview establishes diagnosis; assess substances, drugs, TSH/CBC when clinically suspected
★ **Ask directly about suicide**, access to firearms, protective factors; questioning does not increase risk
Post-CABG anhedonia, withdrawal, fatigue → depression screen; vein-harvest leg edema expected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Imminent danger or **severe malnutrition** → **observation, psychiatric hospitalization**; remove lethal means
Mild: CBT/interpersonal therapy; moderate/severe: sertraline + psychotherapy; pregnancy → shared risk–benefit discussion
★ Urgent suicidality/catatonia/anorexia → **ECT**; psychotic depression → ECT or antidepressant + antipsychotic
Alternatives: **bupropion** (fatigue/hypersomnia, smoking cessation), **mirtazapine** (poor appetite, insomnia)
Continue antidepressant ≥6 months after remission; recurrent/severe episodes → longer maintenance

rows.label: Complications
items: Suicide, malnutrition, functional decline, recurrence
SSRIs: sexual dysfunction, GI effects, hyponatremia; early activation/suicidality monitoring, especially age <25
Bupropion: seizures; avoid with eating disorders, seizure disorders or brain tumor; mirtazapine: weight gain/sedation
Benzodiazepines in older adults: worsen depression, sedation, falls → stop, use antidepressant

rows.label: Prevention
items: Safety plan, early follow-up after drug changes
Taper antidepressants to reduce discontinuation symptoms; avoid antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: insidious consistent deficits; **pseudodementia**: subacute, "I don't know" answers, recall improves with prompting
Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, elevated TSH
Untreated OSA: snoring, obesity, sleepiness → **mood disorder due to medical condition**, not MDD
Anorexia nervosa: fear of weight gain, distorted body image

table.title: Distinguishing persistent sadness
rows: Waves tied to reminders; self-esteem usually preserved
Pervasive worthlessness; bereavement does not exclude diagnosis
Stressor within 3 months; MDD criteria absent

diagnostic-test-accuracy.name: Diagnostic test accuracy
diagnostic-test-accuracy.scope: Sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, likelihood ratios, cut-off changes
diagnostic-test-accuracy.core: Diagnostic accuracy: classification performance against a reference standard; distinguish detection ability from the probability that a result reflects disease.

rows.label: Definition
items: TP/FP: diseased/nondiseased testing positive; FN/TN: diseased/nondiseased testing negative
False negatives → low sensitivity, an intrinsic test property; NPV varies with prevalence

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ ↑Prevalence → **↑PPV, ↓NPV**; sensitivity/specificity unchanged if disease spectrum unchanged
★ Positive above threshold: **lower cutoff → ↑sensitivity, ↓specificity**; raising cutoff reverses
LR+ >10 rules in; LR− <0.1 rules out; **LR 1** → no information

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Pretest odds = p/(1−p); **posttest odds = pretest odds × LR**
Posttest probability = odds/(1+odds); pretest 20%, LR+ 4 → odds 1 → 50%
Parallel tests, either positive → ↑sensitivity; serial tests, both positive → ↑specificity

rows.label: Compare
items: ROC: sensitivity versus 1−specificity; AUC 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect
ROC point nearest **upper-left corner** → best combined sensitivity and specificity

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Sensitive negative** helps exclude; specific positive helps confirm; neither absolute
Case-control sampling → PPV/NPV unrepresentative without population prevalence
Verification bias: reference testing only selected results → distorted accuracy

diagnostic-test-accuracy.evidence: Established statistical definitions; no guideline-dependent recommendation.

dyslipidemia.name: Dyslipidemia
dyslipidemia.scope: Lipid screening guidelines, ASCVD risk calculation, statin therapy indications, monitoring response to diet and pharmacotherapy
dyslipidemia.core: Excess atherogenic lipoproteins drive ASCVD; treatment intensity follows established disease, severe LDL elevation, diabetes, and estimated absolute cardiovascular risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Familial disorders, saturated-fat intake, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis
Premature ASCVD family history, CKD, smoking, inflammatory disease increase treatment benefit

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; tendon xanthomas/early corneal arcus suggest familial hypercholesterolemia
Severe triglyceride elevation: eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis; low HDL alone is not a drug target

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retained apoB-containing particles → arterial inflammation and plaque formation
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → hepatic LDL-receptor upregulation
Familial hypercholesterolemia: **defective LDL-receptor uptake** → isolated high LDL, clear plasma; high TG: milky plasma

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Lipid panel from age 19, at least every 5 years**; earlier/more often with risk
Nonfasting panel acceptable; markedly high triglycerides → fasting repeat/secondary-cause evaluation; Lp(a) once/lifetime
★ **PREVENT-ASCVD**, ages 30–79, LDL 70–189 without ASCVD: replaces pooled-cohort equations in 2026 guidance
Uncertain statin decision → coronary calcium; zero insufficient for deferral with diabetes, smoking, strong premature history
High total cholesterol alone → full lipid panel before treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinical ASCVD (CAD, stroke, PAD) or **LDL ≥190 mg/dL → high-intensity statin**, no risk calculation required
★ Diabetes age 40–75 → **at least moderate-intensity statin**; multiple risk factors favor high intensity
Above LDL target despite maximal statin → ezetimibe; consider PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid
Severe triglycerides ≥500 → address causes, diet, consider fenofibrate/prescription omega-3 to reduce pancreatitis risk
Adolescent obesity + moderate LDL → **calorie reduction/lifestyle first**; statin only if severe or persistent

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease; statins → myalgias, rare rhabdomyolysis, small diabetes-risk increase
Baseline ALT; CK only with symptoms/risk; most lipid-lowering drugs deferred during conception/pregnancy/lactation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mediterranean-style diet, replace saturated fats, exercise, weight reduction, smoking cessation
★ Recheck lipids **4–12 weeks after diet/drug change**, then every 3–12 months; high despite diet → statin
High intensity lowers LDL ≥50%: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH; correct before labeling primary dyslipidemia
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia; treat renal cause

table.title: Risk-based primary prevention and secondary target

eating-disorders.name: Eating disorders
eating-disorders.scope: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge eating disorder, refeeding syndrome, medical complications, hospitalization criteria
eating-disorders.core: Disordered intake or compensatory behaviors require assessment of medical instability, suicidality, and malnutrition at any body size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescence, dieting, weight stigma, perfectionism, trauma; psychiatric comorbidity and family history

rows.label: Clues
items: Restrictive disease: cold intolerance, lanugo, bradycardia, orthostasis, menstrual suppression; amenorrhea not required
Purging: parotid hypertrophy, **raised amylase**, enamel erosion, knuckle calluses; hypokalemic hypochloremic alkalosis
★ **Syncope, arrhythmia, hypothermia or severe electrolyte abnormalities** → urgent stabilization

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Starvation suppresses gonadal axis and reduces cardiac mass; vomiting causes chloride/volume depletion
Refeeding insulin surge shifts phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical interview plus weight trajectory, vitals/orthostatics, **ECG, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate**
Binge: loss of control plus unusually large intake; bulimia/BED require episodes ≥weekly for 3 months
Assess suicide risk, substance use, exercise, laxatives; normal BMI does not exclude severe disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Medical admission for instability: e.g., HR <50, BP <90/60, severe electrolyte disturbance or acute food refusal
★ Refeeding → **thiamine**, nutritional rehabilitation, serial phosphate/K/Mg and cardiac monitoring
Adolescent anorexia → family-based treatment; adults → eating-disorder-focused psychotherapy; medication alone insufficient
Bulimia → CBT plus fluoxetine; avoid bupropion because of seizures
BED → CBT; lisdexamfetamine for selected adults, monitor misuse/cardiovascular risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypoestrogenism → osteoporosis, infertility; cardiac failure, arrhythmic death; purging → arrhythmias, esophageal injury
Refeeding → hypophosphatemia, respiratory failure, edema, delirium; high suicide mortality
Severe starvation → **hypoalbuminemia** with pitting edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early recognition of growth/weight-trajectory changes; reduce weight-based stigma; relapse follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperthyroidism: increased appetite with tremor and heat intolerance
GI malabsorption: involuntary weight loss without weight/shape-driven restriction

eating-disorders.evidence: Guideline framework checked 2026-10-30: [APA eating disorders guideline, 2023](https://www.psychiatry.org/psychiatrists/practice/clinical-practice-guidelines/eating-disorders); thresholds: established clinical teaching.

table.title: Diagnostic distinction
rows: Restriction or purging + weight-gain fear/distorted self-image

elbow-injuries.name: Elbow injuries
elbow-injuries.scope: Supracondylar fracture of the humerus, radial head subluxation, elbow dislocation, fat pad signs, lateral and medial epicondylitis, counterforce bracing, cubital tunnel syndrome
elbow-injuries.core: Age, mechanism, deformity, and precise tenderness separate elbow fracture/dislocation from traction injury, tendinopathy, and nerve compression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fall onto outstretched hand → fracture/dislocation; longitudinal forearm pull → pediatric radial-head subluxation
Repetitive wrist loading → epicondylitis; prolonged elbow flexion/pressure, valgus throwing stress → ulnar nerve compression

rows.label: Clues
items: Pain, swelling, limited motion after trauma; open wound or tense swelling increases urgency
★ **Absent pulse, cool hand, worsening pain with passive stretch** → vascular injury/compartment syndrome
Check median/anterior interosseous, radial, ulnar function before and after reduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pediatric annular-ligament displacement restricts rotation; displaced distal humerus can injure brachial artery
Overuse tendon degeneration differs from inflammatory arthritis; cubital tunnel compresses the ulnar nerve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Trauma/deformity → **AP/lateral radiographs**; posterior fat pad indicates occult intra-articular fracture
Anterior humeral line missing capitellum supports displaced supracondylar fracture
Classic nursemaid presentation without swelling/bony tenderness → clinical diagnosis; image atypical or failed reduction
Nerve-conduction testing for uncertain or persistent cubital neuropathy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Supracondylar fracture: **splint and urgent orthopedics**; displaced/vascularly compromised → reduction and pinning
Elbow dislocation → reduction, repeat neurovascular examination/films, early supervised motion
★ Nursemaid elbow → **hyperpronation** or supination-flexion; reassess spontaneous arm use
Tendinopathy: rest, NSAIDs, rehabilitation, counterforce brace; cubital tunnel: avoid flexion/pressure, night splint

rows.label: Complications
items: Volkmann ischemic contracture, malunion/cubitus varus, persistent neuropathy
Dislocation → stiffness, instability, heterotopic ossification; immobilization worsens loss of motion

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Lift children **under the arms**, avoiding traction on hands/wrists
Ergonomic tools, gradual load progression, stretching/strengthening; pad elbow during repetitive contact

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic joint: fever, effusion, severe passive-motion pain
Radial-head fracture: adult fall, lateral tenderness, painful pronation/supination

table.title: Overuse localization
rows: Medial pain during wrist flexion/pronation against resistance

elbow-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic and peripheral nerve principles.

enterovirus-infections.name: Enterovirus infections
enterovirus-infections.scope: Coxsackievirus A, Coxsackievirus B (epidemic pleurodynia, viral myocarditis, pericarditis), echovirus, aseptic meningitis
enterovirus-infections.core: Enteroviruses cause common self-limited febrile syndromes but also aseptic meningitis, myocarditis and severe neonatal sepsis-like illness.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young children, summer/early autumn, childcare exposure; fecal–oral and respiratory spread
Newborn peripartum exposure and antibody deficiency increase severe disseminated infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Hand-foot-mouth: oral ulcers plus **vesicles on palms/soles**; sometimes buttocks
Herpangina: fever with painful **posterior oropharyngeal vesicles/ulcers**, usually no hand/foot eruption
Pleurodynia: paroxysmal chest/upper abdominal muscle spasms, fever, **elevated CK**
Neonates: poor feeding, hepatitis, coagulopathy, shock or arrhythmia; older children: headache/meningismus

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonenveloped positive-sense RNA picornaviruses survive gastric acidity; replication followed by viremia
Tissue tropism produces mucocutaneous, meningeal, myocardial or skeletal muscle disease

rows.label: Dx
items: Typical uncomplicated exanthem → clinical diagnosis; no routine serology
★ Suspected meningitis → **LP with CSF enterovirus PCR**, bacterial studies and glucose/protein
Viral CSF usually lymphocytic, normal glucose, mildly elevated protein; early neutrophils possible
Chest pain with cardiac concern → ECG, troponin, echocardiography; MRI for suspected myocarditis
Ill neonate → blood/CSF cultures and sepsis evaluation; do not assume benign viral disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated disease → **oral fluids, acetaminophen/ibuprofen**, assess hydration
Unexcluded bacterial meningitis/sepsis → empiric ceftriaxone + vancomycin; neonates → ampicillin + cefotaxime
Myocarditis → cardiac monitoring, heart-failure support; shock → intensive care and circulatory support
No routine antibiotic or antiviral treatment for confirmed uncomplicated enterovirus infection
Painful mouth lesions → cool liquids; avoid aspirin in children

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, myopericarditis, encephalitis; some serotypes cause acute flaccid myelitis
Fulminant neonatal hepatitis/coagulopathy or myocardial failure can be fatal

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap, surface cleaning, diaper hygiene; viral stool shedding can persist
Routine polio vaccination prevents poliomyelitis; no routine US vaccine for nonpolio enteroviruses

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV gingivostomatitis: anterior diffuse gingivitis and painful lesions
Bacterial meningitis: low CSF glucose, high protein; cultures/PCR establish cause
Pulmonary embolism: hypoxemia, clot risk; viral pleurisy → fever, **pleural friction rub**, viral rash
Streptococcal pharyngitis: tonsillar exudates, palatal petechiae, no discrete vesicles

enterovirus-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established infectious-disease teaching.

esophageal-motility-disorders.name: Esophageal motility disorders
esophageal-motility-disorders.scope: Achalasia, diffuse esophageal spasm, hypercontractile esophagus, Zenker diverticulum, manometry, barium swallow
esophageal-motility-disorders.core: Dysphagia to solids and liquids from onset suggests impaired motility; progressive solids-first dysphagia suggests mechanical obstruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Achalasia often idiopathic; Chagas disease can destroy enteric ganglia
Older age predisposes to Zenker diverticulum; opioids can produce spastic motility patterns

rows.label: Clues
items: Achalasia: regurgitated undigested food, nocturnal cough, weight loss
★ Zenker: **halitosis, cervical gurgling, aspiration**, retained food hours after eating
Spastic disorders: intermittent dysphagia and squeezing chest pain; hot/cold liquids may provoke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory myenteric neurons → impaired LES relaxation and absent peristalsis
Zenker: cricopharyngeal dysfunction → mucosal herniation through Killian triangle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Esophageal symptoms → **upper endoscopy** to exclude stricture/cancer before motility testing
★ **High-resolution manometry** confirms functional disorder after structural disease excluded
Barium swallow defines emptying; suspected Zenker → **barium study before endoscopy**
Rapid weight loss, older onset or difficult LES passage → evaluate pseudoachalasia with CT/endoscopic ultrasound
Chest pain → exclude ACS before labeling esophageal spasm

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Achalasia → pneumatic dilation, Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or **POEM**
Botulinum toxin for achalasia when procedural risk precludes durable treatment
Spastic disorders → remove opioid trigger, treat reflux; diltiazem or nitrates for persistent symptoms
Symptomatic Zenker → **cricopharyngeal myotomy + diverticulectomy** or endoscopic septotomy; no dilation or blind NG tube

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition; longstanding achalasia → increased squamous cancer risk
Dilation/myotomy → perforation; myotomy, especially POEM → gastroesophageal reflux

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eat slowly, chew thoroughly, remain upright after meals to reduce regurgitation/aspiration

rows.label: Mimics
items: Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-first symptoms; obstructing lesion
Scleroderma: hypotensive LES with reflux, distal aperistalsis

table.title: Manometry and contrast findings
rows: Impaired LES relaxation; absent normal peristalsis

esophageal-motility-disorders.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG achalasia guideline](https://gi.org/guideline/diagnosis-and-management-of-achalasia/); other disorders established teaching.

esophagitis.name: Esophagitis
esophagitis.scope: Pill-induced esophagitis, infectious esophagitis (Candida, HSV, CMV), eosinophilic esophagitis, prevention strategies
esophagitis.core: Odynophagia suggests mucosal inflammation; episodic solid-food dysphagia and impaction in an atopic patient suggest eosinophilic disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pills taken with little water or before lying down: doxycycline, bisphosphonates, NSAIDs, potassium, iron
Candida: HIV, steroids, antibiotics; HSV/CMV: impaired cellular immunity, transplantation
Eosinophilic disease: asthma, eczema, food allergy; often young men

rows.label: Clues
items: Pill injury: abrupt retrosternal pain after medication; often mid-esophageal ulceration
★ **Oral thrush + odynophagia** supports Candida, but absence of thrush does not exclude
Eosinophilic disease: compensatory slow eating, excessive chewing, avoidance of dense foods
Bleeding, progressive dysphagia, weight loss, or inability to swallow saliva → urgent evaluation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Direct chemical injury or opportunistic infection disrupts mucosa
Type 2 immune inflammation drives eosinophil recruitment and later fibrostenotic remodeling

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **EGD with biopsy** for severe, atypical, refractory, or unexplained symptoms
Eosinophilic diagnosis: **≥15 eosinophils/high-power field** plus esophageal symptoms; exclude alternative causes
Obtain multiple biopsies from ≥2 levels; normal appearance does not exclude eosinophilic disease
Typical Candida can receive empiric treatment; nonresponse → endoscopy to distinguish viral disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pill injury → **stop offending drug + PPI**, hydration, temporary soft diet
Eosinophilic disease: PPI, swallowed budesonide/fluticasone, or empiric elimination diet; assess histologic response
Fibrostenotic narrowing → dilation plus anti-inflammatory treatment; dilation alone does not control disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Stricture, recurrent food impaction, bleeding; rare perforation
Ganciclovir → marrow suppression; prolonged swallowed steroids → local candidiasis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Full glass of water; remain upright after pills**; bisphosphonates require fasting/upright instructions
Immune restoration with ART; rinse mouth after inhaled steroids

rows.label: Mimics
items: GERD: heartburn/regurgitation predominates; may coexist
Esophageal cancer: progressive solids-then-liquids dysphagia, weight loss

table.title: Infectious findings and treatment
rows: Large linear ulcers; base owl-eye inclusions

esophagitis.evidence: Eosinophilic guidance checked 2026-10-30: [ACG 2025](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/eluri_feb2025/); other content established teaching.

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage
Older adults: large-artery stiffness (low compliance) → **isolated systolic hypertension**, wide pulse pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance
Child/adolescent high oscillometric reading → **confirm by auscultation** before ambulatory monitoring or workup

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB (older exams: any diabetes)
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults
Weight loss: largest lifestyle BP drop, ~1 mm Hg/kg; smoking cessation barely lowers resting BP
BP control: largest modifiable stroke-risk reduction; also prevents concentric LVH and HF

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: office high, home normal
Masked hypertension: elevated out-of-office only; secondary causes: abrupt/refractory pressure with renal/endocrine clues

fat-embolism-syndrome.name: Fat embolism syndrome
fat-embolism-syndrome.scope: Long-bone fractures, triade of hypoxemia, neurologic impairment, petechial rash, supportive management
fat-embolism-syndrome.core: Respiratory failure, altered mental status, and petechiae appearing 24–72 hours after major skeletal trauma suggest systemic fat embolization.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Femoral/tibial or pelvic fractures, multiple fractures, intramedullary instrumentation
Occasionally major burns, pancreatitis or liposuction; young adults with high-energy trauma

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hypoxemia preceding neurologic deterioration** after an initially stable interval
Nondependent petechiae over upper chest, axillae, conjunctivae; rash may be transient or absent
Tachypnea, fever, tachycardia; confusion, agitation, seizures or coma
Thrombocytopenia, falling hemoglobin; retinal hemorrhages or cotton-wool lesions

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Marrow fat enters venules → pulmonary microvascular obstruction; free fatty acids trigger endothelial injury
Systemic passage through shunts/capillaries → cerebral, retinal and skin injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; no single definitive laboratory test
ABG assesses oxygenation; chest radiograph → diffuse bilateral infiltrates rather than focal consolidation
CT pulmonary angiography may exclude thrombotic PE but miss microvascular fat emboli
Cerebral symptoms with nondiagnostic head CT → MRI diffusion **starfield pattern** supports diagnosis
Fat globules in urine/sputum nonspecific; not required for diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oxygen and supportive critical care**; intubation with lung-protective ventilation for respiratory failure
Maintain perfusion with careful IV fluids; treat shock and associated traumatic injuries
Stabilize fractures after resuscitation; avoid unnecessary manipulation
Heparin and glucocorticoids not established treatments for manifest syndrome

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, right ventricular strain, persistent neurologic injury or death
Ventilator-associated complications; most survivors recover with supportive treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Early immobilization and timely fixation of long-bone fractures after stabilization
VTE prophylaxis prevents concurrent thrombotic disease, not the fat-embolism mechanism

rows.label: Mimics
items: Thrombotic PE: larger-vessel filling defect, usually no petechial/neurologic combination
Pulmonary contusion: immediate post-trauma focal injury; aspiration: witnessed event or dependent infiltrates

fat-embolism-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

table.title: Trauma respiratory timing
rows: At injury; evolves over first day

foodborne-illnesses.name: Foodborne illnesses
foodborne-illnesses.scope: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens, scombroid, ciguatera, Salmonella, Campylobacter
foodborne-illnesses.core: Incubation time and the dominant symptom separate preformed-toxin vomiting from intestinal infection requiring selective stool testing and antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Food improperly refrigerated/reheated; shared-meal outbreaks; raw poultry/eggs, unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat
Infancy, older age, immunosuppression or vascular disease increase invasive Salmonella risk
Improperly chilled tuna/mackerel → scombroid; tropical reef fish → ciguatera

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt short-lived emesis without fever favors ingested toxin; inflammatory enteritis → fever or bloody stools
★ **Severe dehydration, bacteremia signs or persistent bloody diarrhea** → urgent assessment
Campylobacter pain may mimic appendicitis; poultry exposure supports both major invasive enteric pathogens
Fish toxins: scombroid → flushing/urticaria; ciguatera → paresthesias, hot/cold temperature reversal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ingested enterotoxins act rapidly; scombroid: histamine; ciguatoxin activates voltage-gated sodium channels
Invasive mucosal infection induces inflammation and can permit bloodstream spread
S aureus: **heat-stable** preformed enterotoxin builds in unrefrigerated food; cooking does not destroy it

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild brief outbreak illness → **clinical diagnosis**, usually no stool studies
Fever, bloody/mucoid stool, severe tenderness or sepsis → stool PCR/culture including Shiga toxin testing
Suspected bacteremia → blood cultures; report suspected outbreaks to public health

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scombroid → **diphenhydramine/famotidine**; anaphylaxis → epinephrine; ciguatera → supportive care
Oral rehydration; severe dehydration → IV isotonic fluids; toxin syndromes do not benefit from antibiotics
Campylobacter severe/prolonged or high-risk illness → azithromycin; most mild cases resolve untreated
Nontyphoidal Salmonella: severe/invasive or high-risk host → ceftriaxone or susceptibility-directed antibiotic
★ Suspected **STEC → avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs**; hemolytic uremic syndrome risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Campylobacter → Guillain-Barré, reactive arthritis; Salmonella → bacteremia, vascular infection, sickle-cell osteomyelitis
Volume depletion → AKI; antibiotics may prolong uncomplicated Salmonella carriage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Cook poultry/eggs thoroughly; separate raw foods, rapid refrigeration, handwashing; avoid unpasteurized products

rows.label: Mimics
items: Norovirus: contagious outbreak with vomiting and diarrhea
Appendicitis: focal progressive peritoneal findings; toxin illness usually self-limited

foodborne-illnesses.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC marine toxins](https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/food-poisoning-from-marine-toxins.html), CDC Salmonella/Campylobacter and IDSA infectious-diarrhea guidance.

table.title: Timing after exposure
rows: Vomiting; cream pastries, mayonnaise salads, handled meats

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**
Post-cholecystectomy jaundice + dilated ducts → retained stone/duct injury → **ERCP**; HIDA only for bile leak

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastroenteritis.name: Gastroenteritis
gastroenteritis.scope: Viral gastroenteritis (rotavirus, norovirus), foodborne illness, bacterial enteritis, traveler's diarrhea (ETEC), oral rehydration therapy, dehydration assessment
gastroenteritis.core: Acute vomiting and diarrhea usually need hydration and selective testing; shock, blood, focal pain, or systemic toxicity changes the approach.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sick contacts, contaminated food/water, travel, childcare or institutional outbreaks
Infants, older adults and immunocompromised people have greater dehydration or invasive-infection risk
Pet reptiles → nontyphoidal Salmonella; young infants prone to bacteremia

rows.label: Clues
items: Watery stools and diffuse cramps favor noninvasive disease; fever or dysentery suggests inflammatory enteritis
Mild dehydration: thirst, dry mouth, reduced urine; children → fewer wet diapers, absent tears
★ Lethargy, delayed capillary refill, tachycardia, hypotension → **severe dehydration/shock**
Toddler + high fever, bloody diarrhea, **seizure** → Shigella; HUS appears days later with hemolysis/AKI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intestinal secretion or epithelial injury causes water/electrolyte losses
Sodium–glucose cotransport remains functional, allowing oral rehydration despite ongoing diarrhea

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild self-limited illness → **no routine stool tests**
Stool PCR/culture and Shiga toxin for bloody diarrhea, high fever, severe pain or sepsis
Electrolytes/creatinine for severe dehydration; C difficile testing after antibiotics or healthcare exposure
Persistent >14 days or relevant travel → evaluate parasites; focal/peritoneal pain → imaging for surgical cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Oral rehydration solution**, frequent small volumes; continue breastfeeding and usual diet
Shock/severe dehydration or failed oral intake → IV isotonic crystalloid; reassess perfusion
Ondansetron can enable oral hydration; avoid juice/soda as primary replacement
Moderate/severe travelers’ diarrhea → azithromycin; suspected STEC → no antibiotics
Loperamide only selected adults with afebrile nonbloody diarrhea; avoid children and inflammatory disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Prerenal AKI, metabolic acidosis, electrolyte abnormalities; postinfectious lactose intolerance
STEC → HUS with hemolysis, low platelets and AKI; invasive bacteria → bacteremia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Handwashing with soap/water, food safety, **rotavirus vaccination** in infancy
Norovirus outbreaks: environmental disinfection; food handlers remain off work ≥48 hours after symptoms resolve

rows.label: Mimics
items: Appendicitis/intussusception: localized or episodic severe pain disproportionate to diarrhea
DKA: hyperglycemia, ketones; IBD: persistent bloody diarrhea and weight loss

table.title: Common noninvasive enteritis
rows: Vomiting followed by substantial watery diarrhea

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic nocturnal/supine cough may be sole symptom
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional chest pain → cardiac evaluation; nocturnal burning relieved upright → empiric acid suppression
Infant spit-up + **poor weight gain** → pathologic GERD; pyloric stenosis: projectile vomiting at 3–6 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with regurgitation or **recurrent aspiration** despite drugs → fundoplication; gastrostomy alone inadequate
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → **endoscopy + biopsy to exclude cancer**, then dilation plus acid suppression
Barrett dysplasia → endoscopic eradication; low-grade, older questions: EGD/biopsy at 6 months, even after fundoplication

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

gout.name: Gout and crystal arthropathy
gout.scope: Acute gout, chronic gout and urate lowering, pseudogout (CPPD)
gout.core: Abrupt intensely painful inflammatory arthritis from crystal deposition; gout and CPPD require different long-term prevention despite similar flare management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gout: CKD, obesity, alcohol, purines/fructose, thiazide/loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin
CPPD: older age, joint injury, hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia
Flares follow surgery, dehydration, illness, or changes in urate concentration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid-onset red swollen tender joint, often overnight; fever possible
Chronic gout: tophi on ears/olecranon, erosive arthritis; recurrent flares separated by asymptomatic intervals
CPPD in younger adults → investigate associated metabolic disorders

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Crystal phagocytosis activates inflammasome/IL-1 → neutrophilic synovitis
Most hyperuricemia reflects reduced renal urate excretion rather than excessive production

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ First/atypical acute monoarthritis → **arthrocentesis**, polarized microscopy, Gram stain/culture
★ **Crystals do not exclude septic arthritis**; serum urate may be normal during gout flare
Chronic imaging: punched-out defects with overhanging edges; ultrasound double-contour sign supports urate deposition

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute crystal flare → **indomethacin/other NSAID, colchicine, or glucocorticoid**; joint steroid after excluding infection
NSAID failure → switch class; older exam questions may expect potent NSAID, e.g. indomethacin
CKD/ulcer/anticoagulation → favor steroid; adjust colchicine for renal impairment/interactions; avoid NSAIDs in advanced CKD
★ Urate lowering: **allopurinol first-line**, including CKD; start low, titrate to serum urate <6 mg/dL
Urate lowering doesn't treat flares; continue through flares; may start mid-flare (older exam questions: wait)

rows.label: Complications
items: Gout: destructive arthritis, uric-acid stones; CPPD: chronic degenerative/inflammatory arthropathy
Allopurinol hypersensitivity; colchicine → diarrhea/neuromyopathy
Xanthine-oxidase inhibitors + azathioprine/6-MP → severe marrow suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Urate lowering: **tophi, joint damage, ≥2 flares/year**; first flare with CKD ≥3/stones/urate >9 → consider
Starting urate lowering → colchicine/NSAID prophylaxis 3–6 months; serial urate monitoring; not for isolated hyperuricemia
Uncomplicated first flare → **limit alcohol/fructose**, lose weight; thiazide → losartan; keep indicated aspirin
Before allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01 testing with Southeast Asian/African American ancestry; CPPD lacks crystal-depleting drugs

rows.label: Mimics
items: Septic arthritis: positive culture, bacteremia risk; aspiration essential when uncertain
Cellulitis: superficial inflammation, less restriction of passive joint motion
RA: persistent symmetric small-joint synovitis

gout.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACR gout guideline 2020](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10563586/), [ACR gout education 2025](https://rheumatology.org/patients/gout); CPPD established teaching.

group-b-streptococcus-prophylaxis.name: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis
group-b-streptococcus-prophylaxis.scope: Universal rectovaginal screening (36-37 weeks), intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis indications (prior infant with GBS, bacteriuria, unknown status with fever, ROM >=18h, <37 weeks), IV penicillin G, penicillin allergy
group-b-streptococcus-prophylaxis.core: Intrapartum antibiotics reduce early-onset neonatal GBS disease in colonized patients and those with specified obstetric risk factors.

rows.label: Who
items: ★ All pregnancies: culture; prior affected infant or current **GBS bacteriuria** → automatic prophylaxis

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Screen **36+0–37+6 weeks**; result generally valid 5 weeks
Begin antibiotics at labor or membrane rupture; aim ≥4 hours exposure without delaying delivery

rows.label: Test
items: **Rectovaginal culture**; request clindamycin susceptibility with serious penicillin allergy

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Positive culture → **IV penicillin G**; ampicillin acceptable
Unknown status + <37 weeks, temperature ≥38°C, or ROM ≥18 hours → prophylaxis
Suspected intra-amniotic infection → broad-spectrum antibiotics including GBS coverage

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Planned prelabor cesarean with **intact membranes** → no GBS prophylaxis, regardless of culture
GBS bacteriuria ≥100,000 CFU/mL or symptomatic UTI also needs antepartum treatment
Antepartum eradication of asymptomatic vaginal colonization does not replace intrapartum antibiotics

guillain-barre-syndrome.name: Guillain-Barré syndrome
guillain-barre-syndrome.scope: Ascending symmetric flaccid paralysis, hyporeflexia, autonomic instability, preceding infection (Campylobacter jejuni), albuminocytologic dissociation, IVIG or plasma exchange
guillain-barre-syndrome.core: Rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with reduced reflexes after infection suggests immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy; respiratory and autonomic monitoring are immediate priorities.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Campylobacter gastroenteritis, respiratory viral infection, CMV; typically 1–3 weeks earlier
Rare postvaccination association; infection poses greater risk than routine vaccination

rows.label: Clues
items: Leg weakness ascends over days, paresthesias, back/radicular pain, bilateral facial weakness
★ **Areflexia with flaccid weakness**; sensory complaints usually exceed objective sensory loss
★ **BP swings, arrhythmias, urinary retention**, bulbar dysfunction indicate severe disease
Miller Fisher variant: ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; maximal weakness usually within 4 weeks

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Molecular mimicry triggers antibodies against peripheral nerve components
Demyelinating conduction block most common in US; axonal variants also occur

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serial **forced vital capacity and inspiratory force**; pulse oximetry misses early ventilatory weakness
LP: **↑protein with few cells**; CSF may be normal during first week
Nerve conduction studies: slowing/conduction block or axonal loss; normal early studies do not exclude
Marked CSF pleocytosis, sensory level, or early sphincter dysfunction → reconsider mimics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Admit for telemetry, swallowing evaluation, frequent strength and breathing assessments
Declining FVC, often <20 mL/kg, weak cough/bulbar dysfunction → **early elective intubation**
★ **IVIG or plasma exchange** for nonambulatory, rapidly progressive, or significant respiratory/bulbar disease
Do not combine routinely; **glucocorticoids do not help**
DVT prophylaxis, pressure care, nutrition, pain control, PT; avoid succinylcholine because hyperkalemia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Respiratory failure, aspiration, lethal dysautonomia, VTE, pressure injuries
Residual weakness, neuropathic pain, prolonged fatigue; recovery usually spans months

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prophylaxis; early rehabilitation and immobilization precautions reduce secondary injury
Monitor for treatment-related fluctuations; progression beyond 8 weeks raises concern for CIDP

rows.label: Mimics
items: Transverse myelitis: sensory level, early bladder dysfunction, eventual hyperreflexia
Myasthenia gravis: fatigable ocular/bulbar weakness, normal reflexes and sensation
Botulism: descending paralysis, pupillary dysfunction, preserved sensorium

guillain-barre-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established neurology teaching.

heart-failure.name: Heart failure
heart-failure.scope: HFrEF, HFpEF, acute decompensated heart failure, cardiogenic flash pulmonary edema, guideline-directed medical therapy, neurohormonal activation (RAAS, ADH-mediated hyponatremia)
heart-failure.core: Inadequate cardiac output or elevated filling pressures → pulmonary or systemic congestion, even with a normal ejection fraction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: CAD, hypertension, valvular disease, cardiomyopathy, alcohol, cardiotoxic chemotherapy
Decompensation triggers: ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, missed diuretics, NSAIDs

rows.label: Clues
items: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, elevated JVP, crackles or wheeze (cardiac asthma), dependent edema
S3 suggests volume overload; S4 suggests stiff ventricle
★ **Flash edema**: abrupt respiratory distress, severe hypertension, pink frothy sputum

rows.label: Pathophys
items: RAAS/sympathetic activation → vasoconstriction, sodium retention, adverse remodeling
Low effective volume → baroreceptor-driven nonosmotic **ADH** release → dilutional hyponatremia; marker of advanced disease
Alveolar flooding → V/Q mismatch, widened A-a gradient, hypoxemia
High-output HF: severe anemia, AV fistula (larger fistula → more shunt); HF signs with **normal/high EF**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography**: EF, valves, wall motion; ECG, CXR, BNP support diagnosis
Low BNP argues against HF; obesity lowers BNP, renal dysfunction raises it
Identify precipitant: troponin, CBC, electrolytes, creatinine; evaluate ischemic cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute congestion → **IV furosemide**; hypoxemia → oxygen; respiratory distress → noninvasive ventilation
★ Hypertensive pulmonary edema → **IV nitroglycerin**; shock → norepinephrine ± dobutamine, urgent cause correction
Congested HFrEF → loop diuretic + **ACE inhibitor/ARNI first**; beta-blocker/MRA once compensated; ACE inhibitor → ARNI: 36-hour washout
MRA: eGFR >30, K <5; never ACE inhibitor + ARB; EF ≤35% despite GDMT → consider ICD
HFrEF foundation drugs lower mortality; loop diuretics, nitrates alone, digoxin relieve symptoms only

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiorenal syndrome, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death, hepatic congestion
Diuresis → hypokalemia; RAAS blockade → hyperkalemia, renal dysfunction; monitor creatinine/K

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Daily weights, sodium moderation, adherence; **continue GDMT after EF recovery**
Treat hypertension, CAD, AF; smoking cessation, exercise, influenza/pneumococcal vaccination

rows.label: Mimics
items: COPD: obstructive spirometry, hyperinflation
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia
PE: pleuritic pain, thrombotic risk, RV strain
ARDS: diffuse infiltrates, no cephalization; massive crystalloid + **cephalization/perihilar fullness** → volume overload

table.title: Chronic phenotypes
rows: Sacubitril/valsartan (or ACEi/ARB), carvedilol/metoprolol succinate, spironolactone, dapagliflozin

heart-failure.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACC HFrEF 2024](https://www.acc.org/Latest-in-Cardiology/ten-points-to-remember/2024/03/06/19/22/2024-acc-expert-consensus-hfref); other points established teaching.

heat-related-illness.name: Heat-related illness
heat-related-illness.scope: Heat exhaustion, classic and exertional heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia and NMS contrast
heat-related-illness.core: Heat exposure with neurologic dysfunction signals heat stroke, requiring immediate cooling before laboratory confirmation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Classic: older adults (**impaired thirst**), heat waves, impaired sweating, anticholinergics, limited water access
Exertional: strenuous activity, poor acclimatization, heavy equipment, stimulant use

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Delirium, seizures, or coma** distinguish heat stroke from uncomplicated heat exhaustion
Tachycardia, hypotension, vomiting; sweating may persist despite severe heat injury
Core temperature often >40 °C; lower readings after cooling do not exclude heat stroke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heat production exceeds dissipation → endothelial injury, systemic inflammation, cellular dysfunction
Sweat losses → hypovolemia; excessive free water intake can produce hyponatremia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Rectal temperature**; oral, axillary, and tympanic measurements may underestimate severity
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis, liver enzymes, coagulation studies; repeat for evolving injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, remove clothing, **rapid whole-body cooling**; do not delay for transport or tests
Exertional: cold-water immersion, else evaporative cooling; classic: evaporative; no alcohol sponging; stop active cooling near 39 °C
★ **IV isotonic crystalloid** for hypovolemia; benzodiazepines for seizures or shivering
Avoid antipyretics; environmental hyperthermia has no elevated hypothalamic temperature set point

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, ARDS, persistent neurologic deficits
Delayed liver injury despite initial clinical improvement

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Gradual acclimatization**, scheduled rest, shade, hydration, cooling access
Avoid strenuous exercise during peak heat; monitor vulnerable adults during heat waves

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sepsis: infectious focus, fever unrelated to environmental load
Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic exposure, clonus, hyperreflexia

heat-related-illness.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency medicine teaching.

hemolytic-anemias.name: Hemolytic Anemias
hemolytic-anemias.scope: autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm and cold agglutinins), hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD deficiency, DAT/Coombs testing, peripheral smear, complications
hemolytic-anemias.core: Reticulocytosis, elevated LDH/indirect bilirubin and reduced haptoglobin suggest hemolysis; DAT and smear identify the mechanism.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune disease, CLL, drugs → immune hemolysis; infections can trigger cold-antibody disease
Family history → inherited membrane/enzyme defect; oxidants, fava beans or infection trigger G6PD crises
Coombs-negative newborn jaundice after maternal oxidant drug → consider G6PD; X-linked, Mediterranean ancestry

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, jaundice, dark urine; splenomegaly suggests chronic extravascular destruction
Severe intravascular lysis → hemoglobinuria, back pain, AKI; hemoglobin decline can outpace reticulocyte response
Spherocytes occur in hereditary and warm immune disease; morphology alone cannot distinguish them
Childhood gallstones + splenomegaly + family history → hereditary spherocytosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extravascular: splenic/hepatic macrophage clearance; intravascular: RBC destruction within circulation
Free hemoglobin consumes haptoglobin; marrow compensates unless infection, deficiency or marrow failure limits production
Hereditary spherocytosis: ankyrin/spectrin cytoskeleton defect changes RBC shape → trapping in splenic red pulp

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC, reticulocytes, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin**, peripheral smear
★ **DAT/Coombs** detects immune coating; negative test redirects toward nonimmune causes
Hereditary spherocytosis → eosin-5-maleimide binding test; usually normocytic, normochromic; ↑MCHC supports
G6PD activity can be falsely normal during crisis/after transfusion → repeat after recovery
Schistocytes → evaluate microangiopathy/mechanical destruction urgently, including platelet count and renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe symptomatic anemia → **transfuse promptly** with blood-bank coordination; do not await perfect compatibility
Warm AIHA → glucocorticoids; refractory → rituximab or selected splenectomy
Cold disease → warmth, treat cause; rituximab-based treatment when symptomatic; steroids usually ineffective
G6PD → stop oxidant, treat trigger, supportive transfusion when severe
Hereditary spherocytosis → folate; selected severe disease → splenectomy after immunization

rows.label: Complications
items: Pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis; chronic immune disease increases thrombosis risk
Splenectomy → encapsulated infection and thrombosis; intravascular disease → renal injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ G6PD: avoid **dapsone, primaquine, rasburicase, sulfonamides** and other oxidants
Before splenectomy: pneumococcal/meningococcal/Hib vaccines; infection education and selected antibiotic prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blood loss: reticulocytosis without hemolytic chemistry
Gilbert syndrome: isolated indirect bilirubin without anemia

table.title: Mechanism signatures
rows: Bite cells; Heinz bodies on supravital stain

hemolytic-anemias.evidence: Not checked online; established hematology teaching.

herpes-simplex-virus.name: Herpes simplex virus
herpes-simplex-virus.scope: HSV-1 and HSV-2, genital herpes, neonatal herpes, herpes labialis, eczema herpeticum, acyclovir
herpes-simplex-virus.core: Painful grouped vesicles recurring at mucocutaneous sites reflect latent HSV reactivation; neonatal infection and disseminated disease require urgent systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin/mucosal contact, asymptomatic shedding, new sexual partners; either HSV type can cause genital disease
Immunosuppression, atopic dermatitis; neonatal risk highest with newly acquired maternal infection near delivery

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary genital: fever, tender nodes, dysuria, painful ulcers, 2–3 weeks; recurrences milder, resolve within 1 week
Labialis: tingling prodrome, vermilion cluster; **whitlow**: painful grouped finger vesicles after oral-secretion exposure
★ **Monomorphic punched-out erosions in eczema** → eczema herpeticum; ocular symptoms threaten vision
Neonate: sepsislike illness, vesicles sometimes absent; seizures/hepatitis suggest CNS or disseminated disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: HSV establishes sensory ganglion latency; stress, illness, UV exposure trigger reactivation
Genital HSV-2 recurs/sheds more than genital HSV-1

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Active lesion → **HSV PCR/NAAT with typing**; culture less sensitive as lesions heal
